html:
In 1580 the Mughal Empire brought in a new way of taxing land, worked out by Akbar's finance minister Raja Todar Mal. It paid for the empire for a century and a half.

Almost all state income came from the harvest. Earlier rulers had guessed at the crop each year or shared it on the threshing floor, which invited cheating on both sides. Sher Shah Suri, whom Todar Mal had served as a young man, had begun to measure the land.

The new system was called the dahsala, "ten-year":

  • Every field was measured, with a rod of bamboo joined by iron rings, since rope stretched when wet.
  • Land was graded by how often it was sown.
  • Officials took the average yield and the average price of each crop over the past ten years, district by district.
  • The state's share was one third of that average, paid in cash.

The farmer knew in advance what he owed, and the treasury knew what to expect. Payment in silver pushed farmers to sell in markets (see the rupee). The tax was heavy, and the collectors' records were kept in Persian, which Hindu clerks now learnt.

The Marathas and the British built their own land systems on its records.
sum: In 1580 the Mughal Empire brought in a new way of taxing land, worked out by Akbar's finance minister Raja Todar Mal. It paid for the empire for a century and a half.
